en: He went to settle the account
Of the infidel Sarybai.
He went to begin the strife and break the host,
To be struck by a musket ball and fall,
To perish and die,
To grapple and contend,
And spill without mercy the blood
Of the oppressor who brought lamentation;
To strike and raise the conflict,
And deliver the poor people, once living free,
From this fevered, calamitous war,
And bring them safely away.
The young lion and tiger
Revealed himself a true champion;
He donned his coat no bullet could pierce,
Flicked his eyelids and arched his brows,
And the noble tiger showed no concern.
He did not esteem the monster’s son,
That swine, worth even his boot-heel;
He reckoned him less than a hair and never flinched,
Never stirred in apprehension.
Turning toward the qibla,
He lifted the enchanted spear inherited from his fathers
And aimed it toward the enemy.
With Zulfiqar fastened at his waist,
He invoked the spirits
Of his forefathers who had passed before.
When the gray-maned wolf rode forth,
Ancestral spirits settled upon him in majesty;
He towered like a lofty mountain,
Appearing like a blue-ridged peak,
And all who saw him felt their hearts stirred.
He girded on his fearsome steel
And prepared for the combat,
Calling upon the spirit
Of the magnanimous hero gone to the next world.
The descendant of the sovereign lion
Looked neither up nor down,
And counted the calamity of death
As no more than a hair.
When one gazed at him, the heart was stirred;
If six great rivers turned,
They seemed no more than a cleft in the earth;
The confluence of six streams
Seemed no more than a mountain pass.
When the noble lion grew wrathful,
He seemed able to engulf the whole world;
Even the vast, broad-breasted earth
Seemed unable to withstand
The prince’s valiant son.
Broad-chested and wide-breasted,
The doomed hero stood imposing,
Both a champion and a lion;
Such was he when setting out on that long road,
Like one who had suffered bitter torment,
Like a champion entering the field.
God Almighty in His power
Creates living souls in every kind.
As the youth sat mounted,
The memory stirred his heart:
“Urge your Akkula onward;
Now charge, my son!”
“Where is your heroic courage?”
“Drive your steel-tipped spear
Into the very heart
Of the swine confronting you!
This is the hour to show your courage!”
He had mounted Akkula;
The gray-maned lion, warrior Manas,
Rode beside him as his companion.
Seytek, lion of the bloodthirsty hero,
Seytek, whose fortune was complete,
Dark blue as the sea itself,
Rode toward the clash,
Having received the great host’s blessing.
O almighty Creator,
The cherished young boy
Was riding away to battle;
The sole hero granted as a gift
Was riding away to the fray;
He was going forth to face
Evil and affliction.
“Creator, sustain him Yourself;
Almighty Creator, prosper him;
When the people behold the boy,
May God prosper his deed.”
As the boy rode against the enemy,
The people wailed and wept,
Crying, “Protect, we pray, this boy,
Small as a crow!”
The broad Chatkal of rugged hills
Was no mountain to cross without heed;
Sarybai, oppressor of the age,
Was no foe for a hero to trust lightly.
His champion’s might was well known,
Yet the boy rode straight against him,
Going to the place of cruel calamity
And mighty strife.
With matchless courage and potent wrath,
He rode against the mighty warrior.
When the crow-sized boy set forth,
The people wailed and wept,
Their souls tormented by grief,
Their hearts distracted by care.
Behold the warrior Seytek:
He stood apart beyond all the world,
Trained beyond all the world;
He rode forth like a lion.
Seizing the black-thonged whip,
He swung it around,
And struck Kunansur’s flank
So that it rang aloud.
Kulansur turned his neck.
With a steel shaft and keen point,
The socketed enchanted spear
Was leveled at Sarybai, who had come to single combat,
And now thrust toward the sky.
He roared as he faced the foe,
Raising the battle cry of “Manas!”
As he charged the enemy,
The fearsome youth
Showed the aspect of a tiger.
When he came face-to-face with Sarybai,
With a piercing cry and shrill battle shout
The hero launched his charge.
At one glance he seemed one man,
At another, a thousand men;
At one glance, a radiant chosen steed;
His terrible majesty stood apart.
At another glance, behind the mighty warrior,
A dark-maned black leopard,
The spirit of Khan Manas,
Could be seen.
It had come to ride beside him;
The Forty Holy Ones and Khizr Ilyas
Had become his companions.
Abiding beneath blessed fortune,
They charged in ranks of forty.
Against that infidel Sarybai
He charged and thrust his spear.
When Seytek bore down upon him,
The infidel’s fury redoubled—
Your warrior Sarybai,
The boar who devastated the nation,
The villain long accustomed
To drinking blood,
Who had waged war for many years,
Dominated the whole age,
Gnawed down all he encountered,
And, hardened by bloodshed,
Had become renowned as a bloodthirsty killer.
When Seytek leveled his spear,
And drew near
To the field of combat,
“Look, the boy they rely upon
Has come out to fight!
Now I shall settle the account
Of this ill-fated boy
And beat out his ancient madness.
Before he reaches maturity,
Before his coming day can dawn,
I shall finish him altogether.
I shall see the full courage
Of this boy who boasts of strength,
And carefully spill his blood.
I shall curb his imperious rage
And quench him like a dying fire.
Ravening as I wreak havoc,
I shall crush whoever assails me;
I shall leave none around me alive,
And seize him by both skirts.
You wretch who boasts of courage and lionhood,
Who boasts of strength,
I shall put an end to you indeed.
I shall unleash upon this boy
My fierce courage and surpassing fury.
I shall overcome every ailing foe,
Crush whoever encounters me,
Bend down whoever confronts me,
And defeat whoever crosses me.
If I do not conquer their champions,
If I do not swallow all who ride against me,
Then before Sarybai can be called a mighty warrior,
May I sink away unborn;
May I die rather than live!”
They stood opposed to one another,
And Sarybai, enraged,
Roared and leveled his spear.
At the boy, that wolf of war,
He thrust his steel-shafted enchanted spear,
Aiming it at his liver.
A renowned master among spearmen,
A consummate master of cunning,
He had faced heroes in many lands
And met countless disasters as an equal.
The cunning dog knew well how to thrust a spear;
Though the whole world surrounded him, none had defeated him,
And he was a master of stratagems.
When Sarybai thrust his spear,
He gathered all his strength.
When he thunderously drove the spear
At the mighty gray-maned Seytek,
As the spear came for his blood,
And was about to strike its mark,
The spirit-steed Kulansur
Flickered aside like a hare
And darted away like a wild ass.
The arrow-swift, accursed racer
Would not let the spear reach him;
No wind could match his gallop.
The blessed horse was like a spirit of the wind,
And no beast could match his stride.
He flew whirring like an arrow,
And surged like a flying cloud;
A mighty clatter of stones and earth
Whirled above his head.
He bounded as though shot from a bow,
Soft-mouthed and perfectly responsive;
When he turned, he darted aside,
Before one could cry, “This way or that!”
In the blink of an eye,
Before one could say a word,
Before he could turn Tookyzyl’s head,
Before he could steady himself and thrust his spear,
Brave Seytek, upheld by the spirits,
Had already wheeled his horse around.
Before a word could be said,
Before Tookyzyl could close his mouth,
He wheeled about with a shout,
Raising his battle cry,
And before he could thrust at Seytek,
The descendant of the leopard-lion,
The dark-maned, dauntless lion,
The hero of surpassing courage,
Who had ridden into battle there,
Against that mountain-sized villain,
Against that warrior versed in every ruse,
Against that snow-demonic infidel,
Against that mighty, full-blooded champion,
Who deemed himself a hero and a lion,
Who vaunted himself before the whole world,
The matchlessly nimble warrior,
Turned Kulansur’s neck,
And the spear inherited from his forefathers
The heroic prince leveled.
Such was his valor,
His forefather was a mighty, peerless lion,
And there they met in combat.
At the monster-born warrior,
At the infidel who smeared the earth,
“The face of his belt,” he thought,
“The edge of his right shoulder;
If the tempered spear goes lower,
The rim of his ribs;
Here lies the crown of his heart,
His lungs, heart, and windpipe;
